title: Forgetting is Not Always Bad: A Neuro-Inspired Memory Repair Mechanism for Poisoned LLM Agents
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Existing defenses add overhead or disrupt reasoning; ours adapts a biological forgetting mechanism to selectively decay harmful memories while keeping benign ones.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right flows, biology-to-agent analogy with before/after inset
description: The figure has two stacked panels on grey-blue backgrounds. The top panel, (a) Existing Defense Methods, is split into two boxes. ① Online Auditing shows a robot and a memory-bank server. Memory Scan and Output Filtering arrows lead into an Auditor Module, which outputs Benign (green check) or Poison (red cross). ② Dual Memory shows a robot choosing between a green Benign database and a red Poison database, joined by dashed green and red arrows. The bottom panel, (b) Neuro-inspired Forgetting for LLM Agents, starts on the left with a brain diagram. A weak cue triggers an intrusive memory, then synaptic destabilization, then trace decay with scissors. To the right, a four-step node-graph sequence runs from Memory Embedding through Poison Exposed and Selective Forgetting to Benign Preserved, starting from a Weak Probe arrow. A small Agent Behavior column shows a before state (red cross, warning) and an after state (green check). Red marks poison and green marks benign throughout.
caption: Existing defenses versus neuro-inspired forgetting for poisoned LLM agents. (a) Existing defenses rely on online auditing, which require more computational overhead when continuous scan, or dual-memory isolation, which result in reasoning disruption. (b) Inspired by biological forgetting, weak reactivation destabilizes intrusive memories for gradual decay (left), which motivates weak probing to expose poisoned memories for selective forgetting while preserving benign ones in LLM agents (right).
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are highly vulnerable to memory-poisoning attacks. Existing defenses primarily rely on external modules for either static memory isolation or continuous online auditing, resulting in low memory efficiency and high computational overhead. To address these limitations, inspired by neuroscientific mechanisms that weak reactivation can destabilize memories and induce decay in the absence of reinforcement, we propose an agent-intrinsic training-free memory repair framework, DREAM (Dynamic Reactivation for Engram Attenuation in Memory), that enables selective functional forgetting of poisoned memories. Specifically, DREAM implements a three-stage pipeline: perturbation-induced implicit reactivation to reveal the structural fragility of malicious memories, adaptive anomaly diagnosis based on multi-dimensional activation patterns to detect topological anomalies, and a dynamic memory repair module that selectively suppresses harmful memories while reinforcing benign ones. Extensive experiments across diverse attackers and real-world tasks demonstrate that DREAM reduces attack success rates by over 95\% against backdoor poisoning while preserving strong benign utility. DREAM also achieves competitive robustness against injection attacks. In terms of runtime and token consumption, DREAM achieves up to a 2.13$\times$ speedup and a 37.7\% reduction in token consumption compared with A-MemGuard. Furthermore, DREAM also achieves a task success rate of 92.96\% on poisoned multi-agent systems.
